title: Vibe Coding
lede: Building software you can't write by hand. A few questions on scoping an idea, steering the tool and telling a working prototype from a convincing one.
description: Building software you can't write by hand. Test how you scope an idea, steer the tool and tell a working prototype from a convincing one.

questions.q: What's the most common reason a vibe-coded prototype falls apart halfway through?
options: The wrong programming language
The scope was never defined, so every prompt quietly changes the goal
Not enough prompts
The model's training cutoff
questions.why: Drifting scope is the usual killer. Decide what the thing does before you start asking for it.

questions.q: Your app looks right but one button does nothing. What's the best next move?
options: Ask for a full rewrite
Describe exactly what you clicked, what happened and what you expected
Start a brand new chat
Add more features and come back to it later
questions.why: A specific bug report gets a specific fix. Rewrites throw away the parts that already work.

questions.q: Before showing a prototype to someone else, what matters most?
options: That the code is well commented
That the main path a real person would take works end to end
That it uses the newest framework
That it has a dark mode
questions.why: A prototype earns its keep by proving one path works. Polish everything else later, or never.

questions.q: You're starting a new vibe-coded project. What should you define first?
options: The color palette
One user flow: who does what, in what order, and what 'done' looks like
Which AI tool to use
The database schema
questions.why: A single clear flow keeps prompts aligned. Without it, each request nudges the build in a different direction.

questions.q: The generated UI looks polished but data doesn't persist after refresh. What does that usually mean?
options: The prototype is production-ready
You have a convincing shell — backend or storage still needs to be built or wired up
You need a different font
The model made a mistake you can't fix
questions.why: Front-end demos often fake persistence. Knowing the difference saves you from demoing something that isn't real yet.
